proxy_language: Proto-Algonquian (primary, low-confidence proxy) with Proto-Siouan and Proto-Numic as alternates
proxy_rationale: The Plano complex (c. 10,500-7,500 BP: Agate Basin, Hell Gap, Cody) pre-dates any attested language on the Great Plains by 7,000+ years, and the ethnolinguistic identity of Plano bison hunters is unknown. No language can be tied to the archaeological complex. For a game name-builder, a reconstructed proto-language from the historically Plains-adjacent families is the most defensible stand-in. Proto-Algonquian is the best-reconstructed Plains-related protolanguage (Bloomfield 1946; Aubin 1975; Goddard), with a small, regular phonology and well-attested compounding. Proto-Siouan (Rankin et al.) is a plausible alternative, and Proto-Numic or Proto-Uto-Aztecan for the western fringe. The link is a convention for plausible phonotactic flavor, not a claim of descent. Names should be marked as reconstructed and speculative.
phonology: Proto-Algonquian (Bloomfield 1946; Goddard; Aubin 1975). Consonants: *p *t *c [tS] *k *s *S [esh] *h *m *n *l *y *w, plus *θ and cluster-related *r in some reconstructions. Vowels: short *i *a *o and long *i· *e· *a· *o· (length marked by a following dot or macron). Voiceless stops are the only stop series (voicing is allophonic and not phonemic). Glottal stop is absent from Proto-Algonquian proper. Stress is not phonemically contrastive for naming purposes.
phonotactics: Syllable shape (C)V(C), with short or long nuclei. Medial consonant clusters are overwhelmingly of the type *h + C or *s/*S + C (e.g. *-hk-, *-ht-, *-hp-, *-sk-, *-st-, *-Sk-, *-nt-, *-mp-, *-nk-, *-nc-). Words are vowel-final (verb and noun stems and inflected forms normally end in vowel or in a suffix like *-wa, *-ki, *-ar). Initial consonant clusters are absent; initial vowels are allowed. No voiced obstruents. No *b *d *g *f *z *v *j *x *q. No sequences of three vowels, no geminate-phoneme contrast in the reconstruction (clusters only).
orthography: Algonquianist scholarly transliteration with asterisk for reconstructions. Consonants as written: p t c k s sh h m n l y w. Long vowels as a with macron (or a followed by colon/dot); in plain Latin script use doubled vowels (aa ee ii oo) as the long-vowel convention (as in Algonquian practical orthographies). Recommended game spelling: lower-case, doubled vowels for long, 'sh' for esh, 'c' for the affricate (or 'ch').
morphology: Polysynthetic, head-marking. Nouns are divided into animate and inanimate gender; plural *-ak (animate) / *-ar (inanimate), diminutive *-ensi, locative *-ink, obviative *-ari, vocative *-i. Possession requires prefixes (ne- 'my', ke- 'your', we- 'his/her'); dependent nouns (kin terms, body parts) are always possessed. Verbs are organized in four classes by transitivity and animacy of the object: AI, II, TA, TI. Roots are typically CV(C)- with derivational 'initials', 'medials' and 'finals' concatenated into stems (e.g. initial *mek- 'big' + final). Reduplication marks iteration or plurality in some stems.
compounding: Stems are built from an initial (root/preverb), optional medial (classifier such as 'wood', 'water', 'stone'), and a final. Noun-noun compounds are rarer than derived stems: a modifier initial or preverb precedes the head noun or final. For 'X of Y' constructions, use the locative suffix (*-ink 'at/in') or a possessed noun (prefix + noun-ar), or juxtapose a modifier initial before the head. For 'Y-maker'/'Y-user', use a verb stem with agentive final (*-eewa 'one who ...' style AI-participle) or a nominalized verb. Head-final in modifier-noun compounds; modifier then head.
noun_phrase_order: Demonstrative or modifier precedes the noun (modifier-head); possessor prefix on the head; adjectival notions are usually expressed as verbal initials/preverbs prefixed to the stem. Quantifiers precede the noun.
sources: Bloomfield, Leonard. 1946. Algonquian (in Linguistic Structures of Native America, ed. Hoijer)
Aubin, George F. 1975. A Proto-Algonquian Dictionary
Goddard, Ives. 1979 and later. Delaware verbal morphology / Algonquian historical phonology
Rankin, Robert et al. Comparative Siouan Dictionary project
Frison, George C. 1991. Prehistoric Hunters of the High Plains (archaeological context for Plano)
notes: No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word. This culture is not Diaithiris. All names are speculative: the Plano complex has no linguistic attribution, and Proto-Algonquian (a family reconstructed to roughly 2,500-3,500 years ago in the Great Lakes region) is a distant stylistic proxy only. Names must follow the (C)V(C) syllable shape with no initial clusters, vowel-final or simple vowel + sonorant words, only voiceless stops (p t c k) plus s sh h m n l y w, long vowels written doubled. Avoid the current game strings' voiced stops and fricatives (j, z, d, g, f). Example target forms: 'mekopi', 'nipaaka', 'ahsenaw', 'wapoosi', 'kishepi'.
unit: Plano complex (Agate Basin, Hell Gap, Cody)
